transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, nice to meet you too. I guess I'm here because I just keep forgetting things I really shouldn’t be forgetting. Important stuff, you know? Like my heart follow-up appointments, or remembering to call the clinic back. 

Speaking of that clinic, they have this absolute racket they play for their hold music. It’s this smooth jazz saxophone that just loops every thirty seconds. It drives me up the wall, but it actually reminds me of this little club my buddy Lou used to drag me to back in the 80s. Lou played the trumpet, actually. Not professionally, but he was pretty good. We used to go down there on Tuesdays... wait, maybe it was Thursdays? They had 50-cent wings on Thursdays. 

Anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right, forgetting things. Yeah, it's not just the doctors. Like the other day, I went over to help my neighbor with a repair job on his back deck, and I showed up without any of the right tools! I was standing there empty-handed. Just completely slipped my mind. So, yeah, that's what brings me in.
Are you still able to manage your bills and medications on your own?

Bills and medications? Uh, I'm not really sure, I haven't really noticed any big issues with that, I guess. I just kind of toss the mail on the kitchen counter when it comes. 

Speaking of the mail, they completely changed our route times recently. We used to get it right at 11 AM, like clockwork. Now it's just whenever they feel like it. The regular guy, Gary, he retired a few months back. Great guy. He used to drive this old Chevy Nova on his days off. Beautiful car, cherry red. I had a buddy in high school with a Nova, and we used to take it down to the lake on weekends. We'd fish for bass for hours. Never caught much, but it was a good time, you know? I haven't been fishing in years, though. I should really get my old tackle box out of the garage... but man, that garage is an absolute disaster area right now. I was supposed to organize it last spring and just never got around to it. 

Anyway, what were we talking about? Oh, right, the bills and stuff. Yeah, I don't know, I guess I get to them eventually when they're sitting right in front of me.
Do you need help managing your medications?

Help with my meds? No, I don't think so. I just take them myself. I keep the bottles right next to the toaster so I see them when I'm making breakfast. 

I've been eating the exact same thing for breakfast for, oh, it's gotta be twenty years now. Two slices of sourdough toast and orange marmalade. You know, they actually stopped selling the good brand of marmalade at my local grocery store. The one with the little gingham lid? Now it's all that cheap high-fructose stuff. I tried complaining to the manager—young kid, couldn't have been older than nineteen. Nice enough kid, but he looked at me like I was speaking Greek. Kids today just don't get customer service, do they? 

Back when I worked at the hardware store right out of high school, we would walk the customer right to the exact aisle if they needed something. We had these heavy green aprons with the big pockets for nails and screws. My buddy Dale and I used to see who could ring up a register the fastest... 

Wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right, the pills. Yeah, no, nobody helps me with them, I just do it myself.
Have you missed paying any bills because you forgot?

Missed paying bills? Well, like I said earlier, I just kind of leave them on the counter. But honestly, that's exactly the kind of thing I'm talking about. The forgetting. It's why I came in today. I just keep forgetting things I really shouldn’t be forgetting at my age. 

Like my heart doctor—I'm supposed to have these follow-up appointments, and I just completely blank on them. Or I'll tell myself I need to call the clinic back, and then... nothing. Poof. Gone from my brain. 

It's just like that deck repair I was telling you about with my neighbor. Showing up without the right tools! I mean, I used to work at a hardware store, for crying out loud. You'd think I'd know better. We used to sell these beautiful Craftsman tool sets back then. Real heavy-duty steel, not like the cheap plastic handles they make everything with now. I bought my first set with my third paycheck. Kept it in the trunk of my car for years. 

Actually, I think my son has that set now. He lives out in Colorado. Beautiful out there, the mountains and all. He went out there for college and just never came back east. He likes to hike... 

Anyway, what was the question? Oh, the bills. Yeah, the forgetting is just... it's getting to be a real problem with the important stuff, like the doctors and the tools.
Because of your memory, have you needed someone else to take over paying your bills?

Take over the bills? Uh, no, nobody's taken them over. I'm still doing them myself. Well, I mean, I try to. Like I said, they just kind of pile up by the fruit bowl. 

Speaking of fruit, I bought these peaches the other day from that little stand out on Route 9. You know the one? The guy with the overalls always sits out there reading a paperback. Anyway, they looked great, but they were hard as rocks. I left them in a paper bag to ripen—my mother always swore by the paper bag trick. She used to can her own peaches every August. The whole house would smell like sugar and summer. We had this enormous copper pot she only brought out for canning season. I wonder whatever happened to that pot? My sister probably took it when they sold the house. She always had an eye for the antiques. 

Wait, sorry, what did you ask me? Someone taking over? No, no, it's just me handling the bills. For better or worse, I guess.
Has your memory trouble caused your electricity, rent, or other bills to go unpaid?

Unpaid? Well, I mean, they're late sometimes, sure, but I always get to them eventually. They don't shut the lights off or anything. I just wait until they send those pink envelopes, you know? The ones that say "Past Due" in big letters. 

I remember when the electric company used to send a guy out to actually read the meter on the side of the house. Our guy was named Frank. Big guy, always wore a gray uniform and carried this heavy flashlight, even in the middle of the day. He had a golden retriever that would sit in his truck while he did his rounds. Beautiful dog. Max, I think his name was. Or maybe Buster? No, Buster was the dog my uncle had when I was a kid. Buster was a terror, always digging up my aunt's petunias. She used to chase him around the yard with a rolled-up newspaper...

Oh, but no, they haven't shut anything off. I always manage to send a check before it gets to that point. I just... I need the pink envelopes to remind me.
Have you ever gotten lost while driving somewhere familiar?

Lost driving? No, no, I know my way around town just fine. I've been driving these roads for... gosh, forty years now? 

Though I will say, the traffic has gotten just terrible lately. They put in that new roundabout over by the old high school, and nobody knows how to use it. It's a free-for-all! I was sitting there the other day in my Buick—it's a '98 LeSabre, runs like a top, they really don't make them like that anymore. The seats are like sitting on a living room sofa. My wife hated the color, it's this sort of seafoam green, but she admitted it was comfortable on long trips. We drove it all the way down to Florida once, back in... oh, must have been 2004. Stopped at South of the Border on the way down. You know, with the giant sombrero? Pedro! It's so tacky, but the grandkids loved the bumper stickers. We bought this awful neon pink flamingo for the yard, but the wind blew it away during a storm a few years back. 

But, uh, what were we talking about? Oh, getting lost. No, I don't get lost. I know exactly where I'm going, even if I have to deal with that darn roundabout.
What month is it right now?

Month? Oh, it's October. 

My favorite time of year, honestly. The leaves are just starting to turn over on Elm Street. We used to have this massive oak tree in our front yard when I was growing up. Every October, my dad would rake all the leaves into this huge pile, and my brother and I would jump in it until we were covered in dirt and little bits of dried leaves. My mother hated it because we'd track it all into the house. She had this vacuum—an old Hoover, heavy as a tank. Sounded like an airplane taking off. She'd be vacuuming and yelling over the noise about how we were turning her living room into a forest floor. 

My brother, he lives out in Arizona now. No autumn leaves out there, just rocks and cactus. I went to visit him a few years ago, and I swear, I don't know how he stands the heat. We went to this diner, and I ordered a slice of cherry pie... 

Wait, did you just need the month? Yeah, October.
What year is it right now?

The year? Oh, it is 2024. 

It is funny, I still write 2023 on my checks sometimes. Well, the few checks I still write anyway. Everything is on the computer now, which is just... I mean, I remember when the year 2000 sounded like a science fiction movie. Everyone was in such a panic about the computers crashing for Y2K. My neighbor Phil bought a generator and about fifty cans of baked beans. He stacked them all up in his garage next to his riding mower. 

Phil was a bit of a character, always getting into these wild schemes. He tried to start a business selling those metal detectors you use at the beach. We took one out to the coast once, didn't find a single coin, just bottle caps and a rusty pair of sunglasses. I think they were aviators. I used to have a pair of aviators... loved those glasses. I wore them until the arm snapped off. Tried to tape it back together with duct tape, but my wife told me I looked like a lunatic, so I had to throw them out. I always meant to buy another pair, but you know how it goes. 

Anyway, what was I... right, the year. 2024.
Do you need someone else to handle your finances because of your memory?

Finances? Oh, no, I handle all my own money. Memory's got nothing to do with it, I'm sharp as a tack when it comes to the bills. 

Though, honestly, paying bills used to be an event, you know? Sitting down at the kitchen table on a Sunday morning with a cup of black coffee. My wife used to make these incredible blueberry muffins on Sundays. Real blueberries, none of that canned nonsense. She'd get them fresh from the farmer's market downtown. We'd walk down there early, before it got too crowded. There was this one fella who sold the most amazing honey, kept his own bees out past the county line. I bought a jar once and left it in the pantry so long it crystallized. Did you know you can just put the jar in warm water and it turns right back to liquid? Fascinating stuff, honey. Never goes bad. They found it in Egyptian tombs, you know. Imagine eating thousand-year-old honey! 

But yeah, the bills. I still do them myself. No problem at all.
Because of your memory, has anyone had to step in to manage your medications for you?

Medications? No, no, I handle all that myself. I've got one of those little plastic pill organizers, you know the ones with the days of the week stamped on the lids? 

Mine is bright blue. I picked it up at the pharmacy down on Main Street. That place has been there forever. Old Mr. Henderson used to run it when I was a kid. He always had a jar of butterscotch candies on the counter. You don't see that anymore, do you? Now it's all chain stores and self-checkout lines. I can never get those machines to scan right. The last time I went, it kept yelling at me about an unexpected item in the bagging area. It was just my umbrella! I always carry an umbrella if it looks even a little gray out. Better safe than soggy, my grandfather used to say. He lived in Seattle for a few years, so I guess he knew a thing or two about rain. He had this amazing old trench coat he wore everywhere... 

But no, nobody needs to help me with the pills. I do it all myself.
Because of your memory, have you needed help with shopping, cooking, or getting around outside the home?

Help with shopping and cooking? Oh, no, I do all of that just fine on my own. My memory doesn't get in the way of any of that. I still drive myself to the grocery store every Tuesday morning. 

Tuesday is the best day to go, you know. They restock the produce overnight on Mondays, so everything is crisp. I like to get those big honeycrisp apples. They are so expensive now, though! I remember when you could get a whole bag of apples for a couple of bucks. Now they charge by the pound, and it's like buying gold. Speaking of gold, I saw this documentary the other night about the Gold Rush out in California. Those poor guys panning in the freezing rivers for months on end, mostly finding nothing but fool's gold. Pyrite, I think it's called. My grandson had a little chunk of it he bought at a museum gift shop. Kids love those gift shops, don't they? They always want the shiny rocks or those astronaut ice cream packets. I tried one of those once... tasted like sweet chalk. 

But anyway, what were we... oh, right. No, I don't need any help getting around or cooking. I manage all that just fine.
Have you been feeling down or depressed lately?

Down? No, I wouldn't say that. I'm in pretty good spirits, really. I mean, it's hard to be too down when you've got things to keep you busy. I've been spending a lot of time out in the garage lately, trying to fix up this old push mower. It's a Briggs & Stratton, a real sturdy machine. They just don't make them like that anymore, you know? Everything you buy now is just cheap plastic that cracks if you look at it wrong. 

My neighbor, Gary, he just bought one of those fancy electric mowers. Sounds like a giant hairdryer! He loves it, though. Gary's a good guy, he used to work down at the bottling plant before it closed up in the nineties. We went fishing a couple times up at Miller's Pond. Caught a nice sized bass once, but mostly it's just bluegill in there. Bluegill are feisty, though, they put up a real good fight for their size. Have you ever been fishing up there? It's so peaceful early in the morning, right when the mist is still sitting on the water and the sun is just coming up over the pines. I used to take my kids there when they were little... 

But anyway, what were you asking? Oh, right, feeling depressed. No, no, I feel fine. Just keeping busy.
Compared with a few years ago, do you feel your memory has clearly gotten worse?

Worse? No, I don't think so. I'd say it's about the same as it was a few years ago. Let's see, a few years ago... that was right around the time my brother Frank finally sold his old Chevy. 

It was a '69 Chevelle, beautiful thing. Painted this deep, metallic blue. He kept it sitting under a tarp in his garage for practically a decade. I used to tell him, "Frank, you gotta take that thing out, engines need to run!" But he was always so paranoid about getting a rock chip on the highway. You know how guys get with those classic cars, they treat them better than their own kids! Speaking of which, his youngest, Tommy, just got his driver's license. Terrifying thought, honestly. The way people drive out there today, everybody's just staring down at their phones instead of the road. I saw a guy the other day drift right into the rumble strip because he was texting. Scared the living daylights out of him, I bet. Serves him right, though, you really shouldn't be messing with those things behind the wheel. 

But, uh, what was the question? Oh, my memory. Yeah, no, I remember all that stuff just fine. It hasn't gotten any worse.
Has a family member or close friend told you that your memory has been getting worse?

My family? No, nobody's said anything like that to me. My wife, Mary, she's the one who usually keeps track of everything anyway. She's got this big calendar in the kitchen, writes everything down in red ink. 

She's always been organized like that, ever since we first got married. We had this tiny little apartment over on 5th Street, right above a bakery. Oh, the smell of that bread every morning! It was wonderful, but it made you hungry all the time. The baker, Mr. Rossi, he used to give us the day-old loaves for half price. He was a sweet old man, had this big bushy mustache that would get powdered sugar all over it when he made the cannolis. I haven't had a good cannoli in years. The bakeries around here now, they just don't do it right. The filling is always too sweet, or the shell is soggy. You need a nice, crisp shell that shatters a little when you bite into it. 

But anyway... what were we talking about? Oh, right, my family saying something about my memory. No, nobody's mentioned anything to me. I think I'm doing alright.
Because of your memory, have you needed help with everyday tasks you used to do on your own?

Help with everyday tasks? No, I don't need any help like that. I do everything I've always done. I mean, I was just out back this morning pulling weeds in Mary's garden. She loves her tomatoes, got these big beefsteak ones growing this year. 

She's been trying to get the soil just right for ages. We went down to the garden center over on Route 9 a few weeks back to get some of that special fertilizer. The guy working there, young kid, maybe eighteen, he had no idea what he was talking about. Kept trying to sell me on this organic compost stuff that smelled like a wet dog. I told him, "Listen, son, I've been growing tomatoes since before you were born." You just need a little bit of bone meal and some good old-fashioned sunshine. We used to have a huge garden when we lived out in the country. Grew all our own corn, squash, beans... the deer would always get into the beans, though. You'd wake up in the morning and half the row would just be gone, chewed right down to the nub. We tried everything to keep them out—pie tins on strings, Irish Spring soap, you name it. Nothing works on a hungry deer. Beautiful animals, though. I saw a ten-point buck out there once, just standing in the mist... 

Wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, needing help with things. No, no, I'm still doing everything myself. Weeding, fixing the mower, all of it. I don't need any help.
Have you noticed that your memory is worse now than it used to be?

Worse now? No, I don't think so. I mean, just yesterday I remembered exactly where I put this old tackle box I hadn't seen since... oh, it must have been 1998. We were living near the lake then. Great fishing spot, right off the dock. You could catch largemouth bass all day if you used the right lure. I always preferred those rubber worms, the purple ones with the little white tails. My buddy Al used to swear by spinnerbaits, but I told him they just get caught in the weeds. 

Speaking of Al, he moved down to Florida a few years back. Bought a condo down in Boca. Says the humidity is terrible for his joints, but he plays golf every single Tuesday. I tried golf once, couldn't stand it. Too much standing around, waiting for people to hit a little white ball. I'd rather be doing something, you know? Keeping my hands busy. I built this beautiful cedar birdhouse last spring instead of taking up golf. The blue jays absolutely love it, though they chase all the smaller birds away. Mean birds, blue jays. Beautiful, but mean. They sound like a rusty pump handle when they squawk. 

Anyway, sorry, what did you ask me? Oh, right, my memory getting worse. No, no, it's just fine. I remember everything I need to.
Has your wife started reminding you about your appointments?

Well... actually, yeah. I guess that's sort of what brings me in today. She's been getting on me because I keep forgetting things I really shouldn’t. Like my heart follow-up appointments, or forgetting to call the clinic back. And it's not just the medical stuff, it's everyday things. Like I’ll head over to help a buddy out and show up without the right tools for a repair job. 

I did that just last week with Jim next door. He had this loose railing on his deck, solid oak, beautiful wood. You don't see craftsmanship like that much anymore. Most houses nowadays are just thrown together with cheap pine and finishing nails. Back in the seventies, my brother and I framed houses for a couple of summers. Hot work, let me tell you. We'd sweat right through our shirts by ten in the morning. We used to keep a big metal cooler of iced tea in the back of his Chevy pickup. It was a '69 C10, stepside, painted this awful seafoam green color, but man, it ran like a top. He ended up selling it to a guy who wanted to turn it into a hot rod. Ruined it, if you ask me. Put these giant chrome wheels on it and lowered the suspension. You can't haul lumber in a truck that sits two inches off the ground! Just doesn't make any sense. 

Anyway... what was the question? Oh, Mary reminding me. Right. Yeah, she's had to stay on top of me about calling the clinic back and those heart appointments, because I just keep losing track.
Because of your memory, has your wife had to take over paying the bills?

Paying the bills? No, Mary's always done that anyway, she's got a system with her little ledger book. But like I was saying, it's the other stuff I'm forgetting. That's really why I'm here. I just keep forgetting things I really shouldn't be forgetting. Like those heart follow-up appointments, or calling the clinic back when they leave a message. Or, you know, showing up to help Jim and not having my socket wrench. 

I don't know where my good socket set went, actually. It was a Craftsman, back when they still made them in the USA. Best tools you could buy. My dad bought me that set when I graduated high school. He was a mechanic down at the old Ford dealership on Main Street. Worked there for thirty-five years, right up until they closed the doors. He used to smell like motor oil and Old Spice. They don't make aftershave like that anymore, either. Everything now smells like... I don't know, ocean breeze or whatever. What does an ocean breeze even smell like? Salt and dead fish, if you ask me. We went to the shore once, back in '82. Rained the whole time. Rented this little cottage that had a leaky roof right over the kitchen table. We had to put a bucket... 

Wait, what was I talking about? Oh, right, the bills. No, Mary handles the bills. It's just the appointments and the tools and stuff that I keep messing up.
Has a doctor told you that you have a brain condition, like a stroke or Parkinson's disease?

No, no, nothing like that. No strokes or Parkinson's or anything. My brain's fine, really. I mean, my dad had a stroke when he was... oh, let's see, he must have been about seventy-five. Yeah, seventy-five. It was right around the time my sister got married to that guy from Chicago. What was his name... Gary? Greg? No, it was Gordon! Gordon. He sold insurance, I think. Had this terrible comb-over that would flap up in the wind. I always wondered why guys do that. Just shave it off, you know? Embrace it. Like Telly Savalas. Kojak! Now there was a great show. Who loves ya, baby? We used to watch that every week. Television was better back then. You had three channels and you were happy with it. Now there's five hundred channels and nothing on but people yelling at each other in kitchens. My grandson watches these people play video games on his phone. Not even playing the game himself, just watching someone else play it! I don't understand kids today. When I was his age, we were outside building forts out of scrap lumber we found behind the hardware store. 

Wait... what did you ask me? Oh, right, brain conditions. No, no doctor has ever told me I have anything like that. Just the heart stuff, and this forgetting business.

patient.answer:
Missed paying bills? Well, like I said earlier, I just kind of leave them on the counter. But honestly, that's exactly the kind of thing I'm talking about. The forgetting. It's why I came in today. I just keep forgetting things I really shouldn’t be forgetting at my age. 

Like my heart doctor—I'm supposed to have these follow-up appointments, and I just completely blank on them. Or I'll tell myself I need to call the clinic back, and then... nothing. Poof. Gone from my brain. 

It's just like that deck repair I was telling you about with my neighbor. Showing up without the right tools! I mean, I used to work at a hardware store, for crying out loud. You'd think I'd know better. We used to sell these beautiful Craftsman tool sets back then. Real heavy-duty steel, not like the cheap plastic handles they make everything with now. I bought my first set with my third paycheck. Kept it in the trunk of my car for years. 

Actually, I think my son has that set now. He lives out in Colorado. Beautiful out there, the mountains and all. He went out there for college and just never came back east. He likes to hike... 

Anyway, what was the question? Oh, the bills. Yeah, the forgetting is just... it's getting to be a real problem with the important stuff, like the doctors and the tools.

patient.answer:
Take over the bills? Uh, no, nobody's taken them over. I'm still doing them myself. Well, I mean, I try to. Like I said, they just kind of pile up by the fruit bowl. 

Speaking of fruit, I bought these peaches the other day from that little stand out on Route 9. You know the one? The guy with the overalls always sits out there reading a paperback. Anyway, they looked great, but they were hard as rocks. I left them in a paper bag to ripen—my mother always swore by the paper bag trick. She used to can her own peaches every August. The whole house would smell like sugar and summer. We had this enormous copper pot she only brought out for canning season. I wonder whatever happened to that pot? My sister probably took it when they sold the house. She always had an eye for the antiques. 

Wait, sorry, what did you ask me? Someone taking over? No, no, it's just me handling the bills. For better or worse, I guess.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the memory problems are impairing instrumental activities of daily living enough to suggest major neurocognitive disorder rather than mild neurocognitive disorder or nonspecific cognitive symptoms.

patient.answer:
Unpaid? Well, I mean, they're late sometimes, sure, but I always get to them eventually. They don't shut the lights off or anything. I just wait until they send those pink envelopes, you know? The ones that say "Past Due" in big letters. 

I remember when the electric company used to send a guy out to actually read the meter on the side of the house. Our guy was named Frank. Big guy, always wore a gray uniform and carried this heavy flashlight, even in the middle of the day. He had a golden retriever that would sit in his truck while he did his rounds. Beautiful dog. Max, I think his name was. Or maybe Buster? No, Buster was the dog my uncle had when I was a kid. Buster was a terror, always digging up my aunt's petunias. She used to chase him around the yard with a rolled-up newspaper...

Oh, but no, they haven't shut anything off. I always manage to send a check before it gets to that point. I just... I need the pink envelopes to remind me.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the memory problems interfere with a basic instrumental activity of daily living strongly enough to suggest major neurocognitive disorder rather than mild cognitive impairment or nonspecific cognitive symptoms.

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about spatial disorientation or getting lost in familiar places, which is a symptom of cognitive impairment or dementia, and is not covered by the ADHD symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Lost driving? No, no, I know my way around town just fine. I've been driving these roads for... gosh, forty years now? 

Though I will say, the traffic has gotten just terrible lately. They put in that new roundabout over by the old high school, and nobody knows how to use it. It's a free-for-all! I was sitting there the other day in my Buick—it's a '98 LeSabre, runs like a top, they really don't make them like that anymore. The seats are like sitting on a living room sofa. My wife hated the color, it's this sort of seafoam green, but she admitted it was comfortable on long trips. We drove it all the way down to Florida once, back in... oh, must have been 2004. Stopped at South of the Border on the way down. You know, with the giant sombrero? Pedro! It's so tacky, but the grandkids loved the bumper stickers. We bought this awful neon pink flamingo for the yard, but the wind blew it away during a storm a few years back. 

But, uh, what were we talking about? Oh, getting lost. No, I don't get lost. I know exactly where I'm going, even if I have to deal with that darn roundabout.

doctor.intent: Assess orientation to time to help distinguish major/minor neurocognitive disorder from nonspecific cognitive or mood/anxiety-related causes.
doctor.question: What month is it right now?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about orientation to time (current month), which is a cognitive screening question. This does not match any of the ADHD symptoms in my profile.

patient.answer:
Month? Oh, it's October. 

My favorite time of year, honestly. The leaves are just starting to turn over on Elm Street. We used to have this massive oak tree in our front yard when I was growing up. Every October, my dad would rake all the leaves into this huge pile, and my brother and I would jump in it until we were covered in dirt and little bits of dried leaves. My mother hated it because we'd track it all into the house. She had this vacuum—an old Hoover, heavy as a tank. Sounded like an airplane taking off. She'd be vacuuming and yelling over the noise about how we were turning her living room into a forest floor. 

My brother, he lives out in Arizona now. No autumn leaves out there, just rocks and cactus. I went to visit him a few years ago, and I swear, I don't know how he stands the heat. We went to this diner, and I ordered a slice of cherry pie... 

Wait, did you just need the month? Yeah, October.

doctor.intent: Assess orientation to time beyond month to help distinguish major neurocognitive disorder/delirium from milder cognitive impairment or psychiatric causes.

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about orientation to time (current year), which is a cognitive assessment question not covered by my ADHD symptom profile.

patient.answer:
The year? Oh, it is 2024. 

It is funny, I still write 2023 on my checks sometimes. Well, the few checks I still write anyway. Everything is on the computer now, which is just... I mean, I remember when the year 2000 sounded like a science fiction movie. Everyone was in such a panic about the computers crashing for Y2K. My neighbor Phil bought a generator and about fifty cans of baked beans. He stacked them all up in his garage next to his riding mower. 

Phil was a bit of a character, always getting into these wild schemes. He tried to start a business selling those metal detectors you use at the beach. We took one out to the coast once, didn't find a single coin, just bottle caps and a rusty pair of sunglasses. I think they were aviators. I used to have a pair of aviators... loved those glasses. I wore them until the arm snapped off. Tried to tape it back together with duct tape, but my wife told me I looked like a lunatic, so I had to throw them out. I always meant to buy another pair, but you know how it goes. 

Anyway, what was I... right, the year. 2024.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the memory problem is causing loss of independence in a core instrumental activity of daily living, which best separates mild neurocognitive disorder from major neurocognitive disorder or nonspecific cognitive disorder.

My symptom profile covers forgetfulness in daily activities (S009), but does not mention needing another person to handle my finances.

patient.answer:
Finances? Oh, no, I handle all my own money. Memory's got nothing to do with it, I'm sharp as a tack when it comes to the bills. 

Though, honestly, paying bills used to be an event, you know? Sitting down at the kitchen table on a Sunday morning with a cup of black coffee. My wife used to make these incredible blueberry muffins on Sundays. Real blueberries, none of that canned nonsense. She'd get them fresh from the farmer's market downtown. We'd walk down there early, before it got too crowded. There was this one fella who sold the most amazing honey, kept his own bees out past the county line. I bought a jar once and left it in the pantry so long it crystallized. Did you know you can just put the jar in warm water and it turns right back to liquid? Fascinating stuff, honey. Never goes bad. They found it in Egyptian tombs, you know. Imagine eating thousand-year-old honey! 

But yeah, the bills. I still do them myself. No problem at all.

patient.answer:
Medications? No, no, I handle all that myself. I've got one of those little plastic pill organizers, you know the ones with the days of the week stamped on the lids? 

Mine is bright blue. I picked it up at the pharmacy down on Main Street. That place has been there forever. Old Mr. Henderson used to run it when I was a kid. He always had a jar of butterscotch candies on the counter. You don't see that anymore, do you? Now it's all chain stores and self-checkout lines. I can never get those machines to scan right. The last time I went, it kept yelling at me about an unexpected item in the bagging area. It was just my umbrella! I always carry an umbrella if it looks even a little gray out. Better safe than soggy, my grandfather used to say. He lived in Seattle for a few years, so I guess he knew a thing or two about rain. He had this amazing old trench coat he wore everywhere... 

But no, nobody needs to help me with the pills. I do it all myself.

doctor.intent: Assess whether there has been a decline in independent functioning due to memory problems, which best distinguishes mild neurocognitive disorder from major neurocognitive disorder/dementia.

Help with shopping and cooking? Oh, no, I do all of that just fine on my own. My memory doesn't get in the way of any of that. I still drive myself to the grocery store every Tuesday morning. 

Tuesday is the best day to go, you know. They restock the produce overnight on Mondays, so everything is crisp. I like to get those big honeycrisp apples. They are so expensive now, though! I remember when you could get a whole bag of apples for a couple of bucks. Now they charge by the pound, and it's like buying gold. Speaking of gold, I saw this documentary the other night about the Gold Rush out in California. Those poor guys panning in the freezing rivers for months on end, mostly finding nothing but fool's gold. Pyrite, I think it's called. My grandson had a little chunk of it he bought at a museum gift shop. Kids love those gift shops, don't they? They always want the shiny rocks or those astronaut ice cream packets. I tried one of those once... tasted like sweet chalk. 

But anyway, what were we... oh, right. No, I don't need any help getting around or cooking. I manage all that just fine.

patient.answer:
Down? No, I wouldn't say that. I'm in pretty good spirits, really. I mean, it's hard to be too down when you've got things to keep you busy. I've been spending a lot of time out in the garage lately, trying to fix up this old push mower. It's a Briggs & Stratton, a real sturdy machine. They just don't make them like that anymore, you know? Everything you buy now is just cheap plastic that cracks if you look at it wrong. 

My neighbor, Gary, he just bought one of those fancy electric mowers. Sounds like a giant hairdryer! He loves it, though. Gary's a good guy, he used to work down at the bottling plant before it closed up in the nineties. We went fishing a couple times up at Miller's Pond. Caught a nice sized bass once, but mostly it's just bluegill in there. Bluegill are feisty, though, they put up a real good fight for their size. Have you ever been fishing up there? It's so peaceful early in the morning, right when the mist is still sitting on the water and the sun is just coming up over the pines. I used to take my kids there when they were little... 

But anyway, what were you asking? Oh, right, feeling depressed. No, no, I feel fine. Just keeping busy.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the memory impairment represents a decline from a previously higher level of functioning, which helps distinguish mild neurocognitive disorder from major/unspecified neurocognitive disorder or a nonspecific mental disorder due to another medical condition.

patient.answer:
Worse? No, I don't think so. I'd say it's about the same as it was a few years ago. Let's see, a few years ago... that was right around the time my brother Frank finally sold his old Chevy. 

It was a '69 Chevelle, beautiful thing. Painted this deep, metallic blue. He kept it sitting under a tarp in his garage for practically a decade. I used to tell him, "Frank, you gotta take that thing out, engines need to run!" But he was always so paranoid about getting a rock chip on the highway. You know how guys get with those classic cars, they treat them better than their own kids! Speaking of which, his youngest, Tommy, just got his driver's license. Terrifying thought, honestly. The way people drive out there today, everybody's just staring down at their phones instead of the road. I saw a guy the other day drift right into the rumble strip because he was texting. Scared the living daylights out of him, I bet. Serves him right, though, you really shouldn't be messing with those things behind the wheel. 

But, uh, what was the question? Oh, my memory. Yeah, no, I remember all that stuff just fine. It hasn't gotten any worse.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there is objective corroboration of cognitive decline from an informant, which best distinguishes mild neurocognitive disorder from major/unspecified cognitive disorder when the patient is a poor historian with limited insight.

patient.answer:
My family? No, nobody's said anything like that to me. My wife, Mary, she's the one who usually keeps track of everything anyway. She's got this big calendar in the kitchen, writes everything down in red ink. 

She's always been organized like that, ever since we first got married. We had this tiny little apartment over on 5th Street, right above a bakery. Oh, the smell of that bread every morning! It was wonderful, but it made you hungry all the time. The baker, Mr. Rossi, he used to give us the day-old loaves for half price. He was a sweet old man, had this big bushy mustache that would get powdered sugar all over it when he made the cannolis. I haven't had a good cannoli in years. The bakeries around here now, they just don't do it right. The filling is always too sweet, or the shell is soggy. You need a nice, crisp shell that shatters a little when you bite into it. 

But anyway... what were we talking about? Oh, right, my family saying something about my memory. No, nobody's mentioned anything to me. I think I'm doing alright.

Help with everyday tasks? No, I don't need any help like that. I do everything I've always done. I mean, I was just out back this morning pulling weeds in Mary's garden. She loves her tomatoes, got these big beefsteak ones growing this year. 

She's been trying to get the soil just right for ages. We went down to the garden center over on Route 9 a few weeks back to get some of that special fertilizer. The guy working there, young kid, maybe eighteen, he had no idea what he was talking about. Kept trying to sell me on this organic compost stuff that smelled like a wet dog. I told him, "Listen, son, I've been growing tomatoes since before you were born." You just need a little bit of bone meal and some good old-fashioned sunshine. We used to have a huge garden when we lived out in the country. Grew all our own corn, squash, beans... the deer would always get into the beans, though. You'd wake up in the morning and half the row would just be gone, chewed right down to the nub. We tried everything to keep them out—pie tins on strings, Irish Spring soap, you name it. Nothing works on a hungry deer. Beautiful animals, though. I saw a ten-point buck out there once, just standing in the mist... 

Wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, needing help with things. No, no, I'm still doing everything myself. Weeding, fixing the mower, all of it. I don't need any help.

doctor.intent: Determine whether his memory problems represent a decline from a previous level of functioning, which best separates mild/major neurocognitive disorder from an unspecified organic mental disorder.

patient.answer:
Worse now? No, I don't think so. I mean, just yesterday I remembered exactly where I put this old tackle box I hadn't seen since... oh, it must have been 1998. We were living near the lake then. Great fishing spot, right off the dock. You could catch largemouth bass all day if you used the right lure. I always preferred those rubber worms, the purple ones with the little white tails. My buddy Al used to swear by spinnerbaits, but I told him they just get caught in the weeds. 

Speaking of Al, he moved down to Florida a few years back. Bought a condo down in Boca. Says the humidity is terrible for his joints, but he plays golf every single Tuesday. I tried golf once, couldn't stand it. Too much standing around, waiting for people to hit a little white ball. I'd rather be doing something, you know? Keeping my hands busy. I built this beautiful cedar birdhouse last spring instead of taking up golf. The blue jays absolutely love it, though they chase all the smaller birds away. Mean birds, blue jays. Beautiful, but mean. They sound like a rusty pump handle when they squawk. 

Anyway, sorry, what did you ask me? Oh, right, my memory getting worse. No, no, it's just fine. I remember everything I need to.

Well... actually, yeah. I guess that's sort of what brings me in today. She's been getting on me because I keep forgetting things I really shouldn’t. Like my heart follow-up appointments, or forgetting to call the clinic back. And it's not just the medical stuff, it's everyday things. Like I’ll head over to help a buddy out and show up without the right tools for a repair job. 

I did that just last week with Jim next door. He had this loose railing on his deck, solid oak, beautiful wood. You don't see craftsmanship like that much anymore. Most houses nowadays are just thrown together with cheap pine and finishing nails. Back in the seventies, my brother and I framed houses for a couple of summers. Hot work, let me tell you. We'd sweat right through our shirts by ten in the morning. We used to keep a big metal cooler of iced tea in the back of his Chevy pickup. It was a '69 C10, stepside, painted this awful seafoam green color, but man, it ran like a top. He ended up selling it to a guy who wanted to turn it into a hot rod. Ruined it, if you ask me. Put these giant chrome wheels on it and lowered the suspension. You can't haul lumber in a truck that sits two inches off the ground! Just doesn't make any sense. 

Anyway... what was the question? Oh, Mary reminding me. Right. Yeah, she's had to stay on top of me about calling the clinic back and those heart appointments, because I just keep losing track.

Paying the bills? No, Mary's always done that anyway, she's got a system with her little ledger book. But like I was saying, it's the other stuff I'm forgetting. That's really why I'm here. I don't know where my good socket set went, actually. It was a Craftsman, back when they still made them in the USA. Best tools you could buy. My dad bought me that set when I graduated high school. He was a mechanic down at the old Ford dealership on Main Street. Worked there for thirty-five years, right up until they closed the doors. He used to smell like motor oil and Old Spice. They don't make aftershave like that anymore, either. Everything now smells like... I don't know, ocean breeze or whatever. What does an ocean breeze even smell like? Salt and dead fish, if you ask me. We went to the shore once, back in '82. Rained the whole time. Rented this little cottage that had a leaky roof right over the kitchen table. We had to put a bucket... 

Wait, what was I talking about? Oh, right, the bills. No, Mary handles the bills. It's just the appointments and the tools and stuff that I keep messing up.

No, no, nothing like that. No strokes or Parkinson's or anything. My brain's fine, really. I mean, my dad had a stroke when he was... oh, let's see, he must have been about seventy-five. Yeah, seventy-five. It was right around the time my sister got married to that guy from Chicago. What was his name... Gary? Greg? No, it was Gordon! Gordon. He sold insurance, I think. Had this terrible comb-over that would flap up in the wind. I always wondered why guys do that. Just shave it off, you know? Embrace it. Like Telly Savalas. Kojak! Now there was a great show. Who loves ya, baby? We used to watch that every week. Television was better back then. You had three channels and you were happy with it. Now there's five hundred channels and nothing on but people yelling at each other in kitchens. My grandson watches these people play video games on his phone. Not even playing the game himself, just watching someone else play it! I don't understand kids today. When I was his age, we were outside building forts out of scrap lumber we found behind the hardware store. 

Wait... what did you ask me? Oh, right, brain conditions. No, no doctor has ever told me I have anything like that. Just the heart stuff, and this forgetting business.
